questions.title: Valid Anagram
questions.problem_statement:
Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s, and false otherwise.
An anagram uses exactly the same characters with the same frequencies, but can be in a different order.
Assume both strings contain only lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: Both strings contain the same characters with matching counts.
The characters differ, so they cannot be anagrams.
The frequency of "a" is different between the two strings.

constraints: s and t consist of lowercase English letters.

brute_force.approach: Sort both strings and compare the sorted results.

optimal.approach: Count character frequencies in one pass and verify all counts return to zero.

key_insights: Anagrams must have equal lengths before anything else.
What matters is character frequency, not position.
You can compare frequencies without sorting by counting occurrences.

common_misdirections.note: Sets ignore frequency, so duplicates are handled incorrectly.
Partial comparisons can miss mismatches later in the strings.

tier_targets.1: Nudge them to think about what property must match besides length, without naming counting structures.
tier_targets.2: Mention character-frequency tracking as the right direction, without describing the exact update loop.
tier_targets.3: Describe incrementing for one string and decrementing for the other, then validating all counts are zero.

never_reveal: The exact code for the counting solution
The final complexity before the candidate derives it
Direct instruction to use a fixed-size array of length 26
hint_framework.expected_path: length check -> realize order is irrelevant -> compare frequency distributions -> implement count-based verification

common_mistakes: Using sets and ignoring character multiplicity
Forgetting to short-circuit when lengths differ
Comparing only unique-character counts instead of exact frequencies

follow_ups.variant: What if the strings include arbitrary Unicode characters?
follow_ups.angle: Switch from fixed alphabet counting to hashmap frequency tracking

follow_ups.variant: How would you group a list of words by anagram class?
follow_ups.angle: Canonical signature construction and hashmap grouping

questions.title: Product of Array Except Self
questions.problem_statement:
Given an integer array nums, return an array answer such that answer[i] is equal to the product of all elements of nums except nums[i].
You must solve it without using division.
All intermediate products are guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer.

examples.explanation: Each position uses the product of all other elements.
Every index that is not the zero produces 0 (because the zero is included in their product). Index 2 contains the zero, so its result is the product of all other elements: -1��1��-3��3 = 9.
Each element is the product of the single remaining value.

constraints: All intermediate products are guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer.

brute_force.approach: For each index, multiply all other elements using an inner loop.

optimal.approach: Build prefix products from the left and multiply by running suffix products from the right.
optimal.code:
def solve(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    ans = [1] * n

    prefix = 1
    for i in range(n):
        ans[i] = prefix
        prefix *= nums[i]

    suffix = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        ans[i] *= suffix
        suffix *= nums[i]

    return ans

key_insights: Each index needs information from elements to its left and right.
Division-free means you should precompute directional products.
You can combine left and right products in-place in the answer array.

common_misdirections.approach: Compute total product and divide by nums[i]
common_misdirections.note: Division is disallowed and also fails with zeros.

common_misdirections.approach: Recompute full product for every index
common_misdirections.note: Works functionally but misses the linear-time objective.

tier_targets.1: Nudge them to split each answer into a left contribution and a right contribution, without naming prefix/suffix arrays.
tier_targets.2: Name prefix and suffix product strategy, but do not describe exact loop order.
tier_targets.3: Describe two passes: write left products first, then multiply by running right product in reverse.

never_reveal: Direct instruction to initialize answer with ones
hint_framework.expected_path: nested product per index -> notice repeated multiplication -> decompose into left and right products -> combine in two linear passes

common_mistakes: Incorrect handling of arrays containing one or more zeros
Off-by-one errors when computing prefix or suffix products

follow_ups.variant: Can you solve this when input is a stream and you can only pass once?
follow_ups.angle: Challenges bidirectional dependency and memory constraints

follow_ups.variant: What if multiplication may overflow 32-bit integers?

questions.title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
questions.problem_statement:
Given an array of positive integers nums and a positive integer target, return the minimal length of a contiguous subarray whose sum is greater than or equal to target.
If there is no such subarray, return 0.
All numbers in nums are positive.

examples.explanation: The subarray [4,3] has sum 7 and length 2.
A single element 4 already meets the target.
No contiguous subarray can reach sum 11.

brute_force.approach: Try every start index and extend until target is met, tracking the shortest valid length.

optimal.approach: Use a sliding window with two pointers because all numbers are positive.
optimal.code:
def solve(target, nums):
    left = 0
    total = 0
    best = float('inf')

    for right, val in enumerate(nums):
        total += val
        while total >= target:
            best = min(best, right - left + 1)
            total -= nums[left]
            left += 1

    return 0 if best == float('inf') else best

key_insights: Because numbers are all positive, window sum changes monotonically when pointers move.
Once a window reaches target, you should try shrinking from the left.
Each index only needs to enter and leave the window once for linear time.

common_misdirections.approach: Using prefix sums plus binary search without considering positivity leverage
common_misdirections.note: Valid but adds complexity and can be harder to implement correctly.

common_misdirections.approach: Resetting the right pointer for each left pointer
common_misdirections.note: Revisits work and degrades toward quadratic runtime.

tier_targets.1: Nudge them to maintain a moving contiguous region and adjust its boundaries, without naming sliding window.
tier_targets.2: Name the sliding-window strategy and mention positivity as the reason it works.
tier_targets.3: Describe expand-right-until-valid, then shrink-left-while-valid loop behavior in prose.

never_reveal: Exact code skeleton for the while loop
Direct statement of which pointer increments first in all cases
hint_framework.expected_path: nested subarray exploration -> observe positivity allows monotonic window behavior -> use two pointers -> derive shrink/expand loop

common_mistakes: Trying to use sliding window when array elements are not guaranteed positive
Forgetting to keep shrinking while sum remains >= target
Returning infinity/sentinel instead of 0 when no valid subarray exists

follow_ups.variant: What changes if nums can include negative numbers?
follow_ups.angle: Sliding window monotonicity breaks; needs different strategy

follow_ups.variant: Can you also return one shortest subarray's boundaries?
follow_ups.angle: Track window indices while minimizing length

questions.title: First Missing Positive
questions.problem_statement:
Given an unsorted integer array nums, return the smallest missing positive integer.
You must run in O(n) time and use O(1) extra space.
The array may contain duplicates, zeros, and negative numbers.

examples.explanation: 1 and 2 are present, so the smallest missing positive is 3.
No positive number starting from 1 appears.

hidden_tests.generator: import random; random.seed(42); nums = list(range(1, 100001)); random.shuffle(nums)

brute_force.approach: Sort the array, then scan for the first missing positive while skipping non-positive and duplicate values.

optimal.approach: Place each value v in index v-1 when possible, then find the first index where nums[i] != i+1.

key_insights: Only positives in the range [1, n] can affect the answer for an array of length n.
If value v is present, ideal position for v is index v-1.
After placement, first mismatch index directly gives the missing positive.

common_misdirections.approach: Use a hash set of seen values
common_misdirections.note: Finds answer but violates O(1) extra space requirement.

common_misdirections.approach: Single swap per index without rechecking
common_misdirections.note: Can leave chains unresolved and produce incorrect placements.

tier_targets.1: Nudge them to focus only on values that could matter for the smallest missing positive, without giving index formula.
tier_targets.2: Name in-place placement by value range, without detailing swap loop conditions.
tier_targets.3: Describe repeated swaps until each valid value is at its target index, then scan for first mismatch.

never_reveal: Direct instruction of the precise swap condition as code
hint_framework.expected_path: attempt sort/set baseline -> realize only 1..n matters -> map values to indices in-place -> mismatch scan yields answer

common_mistakes: Trying to place values <= 0 or > n into the array mapping
Infinite swap loops when duplicate values are not guarded
Returning n instead of n+1 when all positions 1..n are correctly filled

follow_ups.variant: How would you return the first k missing positives instead of one?
What if array writes are expensive and should be minimized?
follow_ups.angle: Tradeoff between in-place swaps and auxiliary memory
